overview: A see-through-walls renderer: every render frame it draws translucent boxes over chests, ender chests, dispensers, and droppers (walking the client's loadedTileEntityList) plus breakable cake blocks found by a 5-block-radius block scan. All positions come from world data the server already sent via chunk packets such as S21PacketChunkData; the module only changes what is drawn, so it emits no packets and cannot be detected by packet analysis.

sections.p: One Render3DEvent consumer drives everything. Five boolean options (Chests, Ender Chests, Dispensers, Droppers, Breakable Cakes) gate the draws. The cake scan is a triple loop over a 5-block cube around the player's integer position that compares getBlockState(blockPos).getBlock() against Blocks.cake and boxes each hit; the tile-entity pass iterates mc.theWorld.loadedTileEntityList with an instanceof dispatch (TileEntityChest, TileEntityDropper, TileEntityDispenser, TileEntityEnderChest) and skips whichever type its toggle disables, drawing every remaining entity with RenderUtils.drawEsp. The boxes are the same semi-transparent black (Color(0,0,0,21)) in both paths.

The chests, dispensers, and droppers are tile entities: their block positions are delivered to every client inside chunk data (S21PacketChunkData tile-entity section) and held in the client's loadedTileEntityList from the moment the chunk arrives. The cake scan reads the same chunk block array. So the module reveals nothing the client was not already told — the server broadcast these positions to everyone; the cheat is only that the ESP makes them visible through walls. A server cannot observe the drawing, so the only real countermeasures in the corpus are the X-ray family, which target the mining behavior that seeing-through-walls enables rather than the rendering itself.

files.label: BlockESP.java
files.explanation: The constructor registers five toggles. eventConsumer0 first runs the optional cake scan — a 10x10x10 cube centered on the player, which means roughly 1000 getBlockState lookups per frame, each hitting the client's chunk block-array cache; then the tile-entity loop, which is the cheap path since loadedTileEntityList is already populated by chunk loading. Both render paths funnel into RenderUtils (box for the scanned blocks, drawEsp for the tile entities) with the same translucent black fill. No packet is read or written beyond what the render thread already consumes.

countering.label: XRayCheck (ore-targeting ghost-block ledger)
countering.explanation: Jinky's X-ray check is the closest real detector of 'client sees blocks it should not'. When a player breaks an ore, the check walks back along the player's look vector through the block column (getopposite from yaw, up to 9 blocks): if the ore sits behind more than two non-xray-safe blocks with no clear line, the check plants a 'ghost block' — it temporarily swaps the covering block's material to the ore type on the server — and then tracks whether the player turns toward and breaks that ghost. Approaching the ghost (closecount rising per move) and finally breaking it flags 'broke ghostblocks 5+ blocks ret'. Honest note: the technique is a behavioral test for ore-mining knowledge, not a packet test; BlockESP renders tile-entity containers and cakes rather than ores and never mines them, so the ghost ledger cannot fire on it. It is the only real check in the corpus that polices the see-through-walls behavior class this module belongs to.

countering.label: XRayProtocol (registration stub)
countering.explanation: Negativity's X-ray protocol class is, in the mined corpus, a 13-line registration stub: it registers the XRAY cheat with its display category (WORLD) and emerald-ore icon and nothing else — the detection body is not present in this build. Honest note: it is included because it is the named X-ray detector in one of the corpus anticheats, and to make explicit that even a major anticheat's X-ray feature is registration-only against a rendering cheat. Like the Jinky check, any real X-ray detection is behavioral (mining patterns), which a pure ESP module never exercises.

countering.label: PacketWorld (per-player chunk-change ledger)
countering.explanation: Spartan's per-player mirror of the server-side world. worldChange records every ServerBlockChange into a query list (with a transactionLock and a 3-tick lag guard so changes apply in order), getBlockRaw consults that pending-change list first with a 1.3-block proximity match, and getBlock falls back to the async chunk cache; tick() expires stale entries once the tick delay is healthy. This is the server-side counterpart of the world state BlockESP reads client-side from chunk packets: Spartan keeps its own authoritative copy of every block the player could have seen, which is what lets its world checks (scaffold, phase, liquid) validate actions against the real layout instead of trusting the client. Honest note: the module's rendering consumes the client copy of that same world; the check family built on PacketWorld is how a server answers 'what did the client actually know about this block' — the question ESP cheats try to make irrelevant.

countering.label: ServerBlock (block-state cache wrapper)
countering.explanation: ServerBlock is the cache wrapper around the block objects Spartan resolves per location: it accepts a Bukkit Block, a Material, or a BlockData and resolves getType() through the chunk-load check (ChunksEvent.isLoaded), returning an empty-material sentinel when the chunk is not loaded, plus isLiquid/isWaterLogged helpers used by the liquid checks. Honest note: like PacketWorld, this is world-truth infrastructure rather than a detector — the pair of files shows the mechanism by which Spartan knows the real block type at any position, which is the server-side ground truth that a client-side block ESP cannot influence and that all of Spartan's world-validating checks depend on.
